Circle On Cevian

GeometryCirclesTriangles
Game: Drag the triangle and the dots on its sides to watch circles follow the lines from its corners.
How to play: Drag a corner or a side dot with a mouse or finger, or focus one and use the arrow keys. Press 1, 2 or 3 to show more circles.
Look for the math

A line from a corner of a triangle to the opposite side is a cevian. Draw a circle whose diameter is one of those lines and something surprising happens: however you drag the corners and the side points, the circles' common lines all go through the very same point.

The circle finds an altitude

Take the circle with the line CPc as its diameter, where Pc lies on AB. Let it meet AB again at Hc. The angle C Hc Pc sits on a diameter, so it is a right angle by Thales' theorem. That makes CHc perpendicular to AB: it is an altitude. The same is true at the other two corners, and the small right-angle marks in the picture show just that.

Equal power at the meeting point

The altitudes from A and C meet at H, the orthocenter. The power of H in the circle on APa is AH · HHa, and in the circle on CPc it is CH · HHc, taking lengths along the altitudes. The right triangles AHHc and CHHa are similar, so CH · HHc = AH · HHa. Equal powers put H on the radical axis of the two circles: that is the green line you see.

Two cevians, one line

So the theorem is: circles drawn on two cevians from different corners as diameters have a radical axis that passes through the orthocenter. The old applet joins the two points where the circles cross to draw this line. Here the same line is drawn even when the circles do not cross, because the radical axis exists for any two circles. The logic test checks the equal powers and the line through the crossings on hundreds of triangles, including obtuse ones where an altitude foot lies outside its side.

Three circles, one center

Add the third circle on BPb. Every pair now gives a radical axis, and all three go through H, which is the radical center unless the circles are coaxal, in which case the three lines coincide. A cousin of this result is the Gauss–Bodenmiller theorem: for a complete quadrilateral, the circles on its three diagonals are coaxal.

Try dragging a side dot all the way to an end of its side: the circle changes a lot, but the green line still passes through the same point.

Puzzle by Alexander Bogomolny (cut-the-knot.org)
